nameStory: Water lobelia gets its name from its aquatic lifestyle and its membership in the lobelia family, named after Belgian botanist Matthias de Lobel. The 'water' part is obvious once you see this plant growing completely submerged in pristine New England lakes with only its flower spikes poking above the surface. Its other name, Dortmann's cardinalflower, honors German botanist Johann Dortmann who first described this unusual aquatic relative of the more familiar red cardinal flower.
description: Water lobelia is a fascinating aquatic plant that spends its entire life underwater except when blooming. It grows as a rosette of unusual tube-like leaves anchored to lake bottoms, reaching 2-6 feet tall when its flowering spike emerges above the water surface. The small white to pale pink flowers cluster along the top portion of this spike, creating a delicate display that seems to float on the water. This is one of the few true aquatic flowering plants you'll encounter in New England's cleanest lakes.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, fleshy leaves that feel almost cylindrical like tiny green sausages, growing in a basal rosette completely underwater. Break one gently and you'll see milky white sap ooze out - a key identifying feature.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white to pale pink tubular flowers with five lobes, clustered in groups of 1-10 along a spike that emerges above water. Each flower is about half an inch long with an irregular, somewhat orchid-like shape.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as an underwater rosette anchored to the lake bottom, with only the flowering spike breaking the water surface during blooming season. The entire plant except flowers lives a completely submerged lifestyle.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small capsules about quarter-inch long that split open to release tiny seeds. These develop on the flower spike above water after blooming finishes.

habitat: Found only in the cleanest, most pristine lakes and ponds with sandy or rocky bottoms throughout New England. This plant is extremely sensitive to pollution and serves as an indicator of excellent water quality. Look for it in clear, nutrient-poor waters where it grows completely submerged along shorelines and shallow areas.

seasonality.spring: Underwater rosettes become more visible as ice melts and water clears. New growth begins but flowering spikes haven't yet emerged above water surface.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season when the distinctive flower spikes emerge above water, making this the best time for identification. Flowers typically appear from July through August.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules mature above water. Underwater leaves remain green and visible through the clear water as an evergreen rosette.
seasonality.winter: Leaves remain evergreen underwater beneath the ice, though they're obviously hard to observe during frozen periods. The plant continues photosynthesis even under ice.

funFact: Water lobelia has mastered an incredible botanical trick - instead of getting carbon dioxide from the air like most plants, it actually extracts CO2 from lake sediments through its roots and pumps it up through those hollow, tube-like leaves to fuel photosynthesis underwater!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other underwater plants like water milfoil or pondweeds, but water lobelia's thick, cylindrical leaves with milky sap are unique. Remember: if you gently break a leaf and see white milky sap, plus the leaves feel like thick green tubes, you've found water lobelia.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name including 'lobelia,' this aquatic plant lives a completely different lifestyle from its terrestrial cousins like cardinal flower. The name 'isoetid' mentioned by botanists refers to its superficial resemblance to quillworts (Isoetes), though they're unrelated - it's a case of similar environments creating similar-looking plants.
compareHints: Unlike its showy red cousin cardinal flower or the tall blue spikes of great blue lobelia, water lobelia is the only member of the lobelia family that lives completely underwater. While other lobelias have typical flat leaves and grow in moist soil, water lobelia has evolved those unique cylindrical, hollow leaves for its aquatic lifestyle. The milky sap is shared with other lobelias, but the underwater habitat and leaf shape make this species unmistakable.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Cardinal flower stands out dramatically from its lobelia relatives—while great blue lobelia produces similar tubular flowers in blue, and Indian tobacco has tiny pale flowers, only cardinal flower blazes in brilliant red.
Unlike its showier relatives cardinal flower (bright red) and great blue lobelia (deep blue), Indian tobacco has much smaller, paler flowers.
Among New England's lobelias, great blue lobelia is easily distinguished by its brilliant blue color and robust size.
Among New England's lobelias, pale-spiked lobelia is the wallflower of the family with its subtle white or pale blue flowers.
Kalm's lobelia is much smaller and more delicate than its showy relatives like cardinal flower (bright red) or great blue lobelia (deep blue, much larger).
Garden lobelia is much smaller and more delicate than its New England native relatives like cardinal flower and great blue lobelia, which are tall, upright wetland plants.

Unlike its native Lobelia relatives such as cardinal flower or great blue lobelia which grow as upright leafy stems with showy flower spikes, matted pratia is a tiny mat-forming groundcover with individual star-shaped flowers.
Nuttall's lobelia is much smaller and more delicate than its famous relatives like cardinal flower (bright red) or great blue lobelia (deep blue and tall).
